newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FEATURE - Czech Senate polls become referendum on Klaus.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Czech Senate polls become referendum on Klaus.

text.p: Six months ago this weekend's Czech Senate elections seemed likely to be a political sideshow. But that was before Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus lost his parliamentary majority.
The polls for a newly created upper house, the first round of which will be held on Friday and Saturday, now look more like a referendum on central Europe's only conservative premier.
Opinion polls suggest a tight race, although Klaus and his Civic Democratic Party (ODS) seem to be edging ahead due to an outbreak of squabbling among the opposition Social Democrats.

If Klaus wins well, he may be tempted to provoke early lower house elections next year to try to regain the majority he lost in the spring and beat off his archrival, Social Democrat chairman Milos Zeman.
If he loses, the career of the man who led Czech economic reform since the 1989 fall of communism might soon be over.

ODS deputy chairman Ivan Pilip has played down the possibility of early lower house polls whether his party wins or loses the Senate. But Jiri Pehe, head of research at the Open Media Reseach Institute in Prague, is not so sure.
"If the Social Democrats win, I can't imagine Klaus and his government continuing to exist," he said. "With minorities in both chambers they would have to resign.
If ODS win Klaus might try to force early polls. "There would be both the momentum and temptation to do so," Pehe said.

At present the Czech Republic has only a single chamber parliament. However, the constitution written when Czechoslovakia split in two at the start of 1993 called for a Senate as well as the lower Chamber of Deputies.
After considerable political footdragging, not least by Klaus himself, only now is the upper house being elected.
The Senate will have few constitutional powers and the rules are likely to attract thoughtful elder statesmen rather than young, aggressive politicians on the rise.
For a start, you have to be 40 to run. Candidates include former dissident Vaclav Benda, Czech ambassador to Washington Michael Zantovsky and top banker Richard Salzmann.
Opinion polls indicate turnout may be relatively low, maybe because Czechs are voting for the second time in six months.
But the political elite will be watching the result for indicators on the future of Klaus, who is now in some trouble.

Before the lower house polls at the end of May, the 55-year-old economics professor seemed invincible. His coalition had made sweeping economic reforms and reduced inflation to single digits, the economy was growing nicely and unemployment was almost neglible.
But Zeman's Social Democrats sprang a major surprise and the three-party Klaus coalition won only 99 of the 200 seats.
Since then Zeman has used his position as speaker of the Chamber to wage a guerrilla war against Klaus, a personal enemy from days before either man entered politics.
Things have got worse for Klaus. The ODS's opinion poll lead over the Social Democrats vanished with most putting the parties neck and neck with about 26 percent support.
Economic growth forecasts are being cut, the trade deficit is soaring and inflation at nine percent has stopped falling.
A number of small banks have also collapsed, some amid allegations of political involvement, and Klaus admits he is under heavy pressure even from within his coalition.

Commenting on one poll, he said: "I consider it to be a great result that the ODS has the support of 26.2 percent now after unbelievable pressure from all sides, claiming our responsibility for the collapse of one bank or another...
"How we will answer the incessant attacks against the ODS, also from our coalition partners, will be a matter for debate."
But paradoxically Klaus has an ally in the opposition and, just as they caught up with the ODS for the first time, the Social Democrats started squabbling in public.
Four prominent Social Democrats, including a vice chairman Karel Machovec, defied Zeman last month by voting with the government on the first reading of the 1997 state budget.
Some deputies started attacking the communist pasts of party colleagues and Zeman added fuel to the flames by threatening to quit next spring unless Machovec went first.

Klaus was quick to exploit on their embarrassment and an opinion poll taken in October showed voters were starting to lose patience. The Social Democrats lost their narrow lead to trail ODS by five percentage points with just 20.2 percent.

But the Senate will be elected under a British-style first past the post system rather than proportional representation used for the lower house. Czechs are unused to this and in any case nobody -- politicians, pollsters or journalists -- forecast that the coalition would lose its majority last spring.
The new system virtually guarantees a showdown between the ODS and Social Democrats.
Candidates have to win over half the vote and most if not all the 81 constituencies are likely to be decided in a second round run-off scheduled for November 22 and 23.
Klaus says he is in no mood for surrender. "The government intends to rule and not to yield to the opposition or even consider resigning," he told a recent rally.
